title: The equation the paper actually solves

cues.text: Take the value curve and stand at one point on it. Close up, the tangent is a good description of the curve.
But it is not perfect. Move a little way, and the real curve has lifted off the tangent — by an amount that depends on the bend.
Which gives the line the appendix opens with. The expected change in value has two pieces.
The first is the tangent's answer: the slope, times how far you moved.
The second is the correction for the bend: a half of the second gradient, times the square of the step. And we know what that square is — it is the one thing randomness leaves behind.
Put the two facts from the last chapter in, and every piece of it is now something we have already built.
The chance to build is an asset you are holding. It pays you nothing while you hold it — no rent, no revenue — so all it can offer is the gain in its own value.
And your money could have been earning the ordinary return somewhere else. In equilibrium those two must match, or nobody would hold it.
Expected gain equals the normal return. One line.
Every single term has a d t in it. So divide the whole line by d t, and every d t disappears at once.

Tidy it up, bring everything to one side, and this is equation A one of the appendix. It is the whole of the paper's mathematics in a single line, and you have just watched every piece of it being built.
Read it left to right. A bend term, carrying the choppiness.
A slope term, carrying the drift.
And the ordinary return being given up by holding on.
close up, a curve is a tangent plus a bend
so E[dV] has a slope term and a bend term
waiting pays nothing, so gain = normal return
divide by the slice, and the equation is left
